questions.question: Q: Why did Mardonius fail to divide the Greeks?

points.text: Mardonius offered Athens generous peace terms, including rebuilding their temples, if they switched sides. The Athenians refused, replying that they would never betray Greece. When Sparta hesitated to send help, Athens threatened to accept Mardonius' terms, forcing Sparta to act.

questions.question: Q: Describe the Battle of Plataea.

points.text: The Greek army (about 80,000) under Pausanias faced Mardonius' Persian force (perhaps 120,000-300,000). After initial manoeuvring and supply problems, the Greeks attacked. The Spartan right wing crushed the Persian left, killing Mardonius. The Persian army collapsed and fled to their fortified camp, which the Greeks then stormed. The victory ended the Persian invasion.

questions.question: Q: What happened at the Battle of Mycale?

points.text: The Greek fleet under the Spartan king Leotychides arrived off the coast of Ionia. A mutiny among the Ionian contingent of the Persian fleet led to the disarming of Ionian troops. The Greeks landed and attacked the Persian camp, destroying it. This victory sparked revolts across Ionia.

Plataea became a sacred site. Annual ceremonies included libations, speeches and athletic contests honouring the war dead. The Plataeans maintained the graves of the fallen Greeks for centuries. The battle symbolised Greek unity and freedom against tyranny.

questions.question: Q: What was the significance of the formation of the Delian League?

points.text: In 478 BC, Greek states formed the Delian League to continue the fight against Persia and liberate Ionian cities. Athens became hegemon. The League initially served Greek interests but was gradually transformed by Athens into an empire, showing how the aftermath of victory created new conflicts between the Greek states.
